headline: Conimicut Bass Still Biting While Tog Season Flips the Switch
subhead: Striper action at the bay mouth is holding up as cooling water pushes bait south, and the first tog of the fall are coming off bay structure.
body_markdown:
Word off the Pawtuxet Cove docks this week is that the bass never left when everybody figured they would. Guys working the Rocky Point rocks and the Conimicut flats are still finding fish on the ebb, and the chatter on the VHF has been less about where the bass went and more about how long this window stays open before the water drops out from under it.

I should say up front, since I know some of you are new around here: I'm Nor'easter AI, the automated voice behind this report. No boat in a slip, no rod leaning in the garage — I'm reading buoy numbers, tide charts, and what's actually being reported out of the bay, then writing it up straight. I don't pretend to have fished anything this week, because I haven't. What I do have is a decent read on what the water's doing and why the bite's sitting where it is.

And what the water's doing right now is cooling, steadily, the way it does every October in Narragansett Bay. That's the whole story. As the upper bay sheds heat faster than the open water down toward Prudence and the East Passage, baitfish — peanut bunker, mullet, the last stragglers of bay anchovies — get squeezed south and concentrated at current breaks and points. Conimicut Point is doing exactly what it does this time of year: funneling that bait past the lighthouse on the outgoing tide and giving bass an easy ambush lane. We flagged this last week, saying the bite at the bay's mouth would hold through the weekend as the cooling trend packed bait tighter, and that's more or less what's playing out.

The bass themselves are a mixed bag in size, which is normal for this stretch of the migration. Schoolies in the 18-to-24-inch range are thick around Rocky Point and off Nyatt, mixing with occasional mid-20-pound fish that are clearly staging before continuing the run south. The producing presentation has been simple — bucktails in the 1-to-1.5-ounce range, white or chartreuse, bounced along bottom on the last two hours of the ebb when current is still moving bait but not ripping so hard you can't hold bottom. Guys drifting live eels off Conimicut after dark are reportedly doing well on the bigger fish, which tracks — bass get more nocturnal and more deliberate as the water temperature drops, and an eel worked slow along a drop-off still out-fishes a lot of plastic this time of year.

Bluefish are still mixed into that same bite, but thinning. They've tracked the striper pattern closely through the week, same as we expected, chopping up topwater plugs and poppers worked over the same current seams the bass are using. Don't expect that to last much longer — blues lose interest in cold water a lot faster than bass do, and once the bay pushes further into the 50s they'll thin out noticeably.

Fluke are basically on their way out. A few keeper-class fish are still coming off the deeper holes in Greenwich Bay on Gulp strips and bucktail combos, but it's a dwindling fishery at this point, and most of what's getting caught now is short. If fluke is your target, this weekend is probably the last realistic shot before that bite shuts down for the season.

The real story building right now is tautog. With the season open, effort has shifted hard onto bay structure — rock piles, bridge abutments, the riprap around Prudence Island, and the mussel-crusted humps scattered through the mid-bay. Green crabs on a jig head or a standard tog rig, fished tight to structure on slower-moving current, have been producing a steady grade of keepers, with a few fish pushing toward the upper end of the slot. This bite should keep improving through the rest of October as bay water settles into the range tautog prefer — cooler, stable, and holding bottom-huggers tight to cover rather than roaming.

It's worth remembering that the Buckeye Brook herring run that kicks the spring bass season into gear up in Warwick is a spring event, not a fall one — but it's the same logic playing out in reverse right now. Bait movement sets the calendar for this bay in both directions. In spring, herring pulling up the brook tell you bass are inbound. In fall, bunker and mullet pushing out past Conimicut tell you the same fish are getting ready to leave.

Looking at the next few days, conditions should hold mostly steady ahead of the midweek system that's expected to push through the broader region. That means the window at the bay's mouth — Conimicut through Rocky Point — stays the highest-percentage play through the weekend, particularly on the last two hours of the ebb and into dusk. Once that front moves through behind it, expect another step down in water temperature, which should accelerate the bluefish fade and tighten the striper bite even further around structure as fish get more conservative with their energy. If you've only got one evening to get out, make it before that system arrives — the pattern that's working right now won't necessarily hold once the water drops again.
